entries.623997d8c3c8acdb30a8aaa1c82df7a9a4f732cf: <div sID="gen15598" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Isa.7" sID="Isa.7"/> <div eID="gen15598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15599" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15600" type="x-p"/> This chapter is an occasional sermon, in which the prophet sings both of mercy and judgment to those that did not perceive or understand either; he piped unto them, but they danced not, mourned unto them, but they wept not. Here is, I. The consternation that Ahaz was in upon an attempt of the confederate forces of Syria and Israel against Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.1-Isa.7.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The assurance which God, by the prophet, sent him for his encouragement, that the attempt should be defeated and Jerusalem should be preserved, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.3-Isa.7.9">ver. 3-9</reference>. III. The confirmation of this by a sign which God gave to Ahaz, when he refused to ask one, referring to Christ, and our redemption by him, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.10-Isa.7.16">ver. 10-16</reference>. IV. A threatening of the great desolation that God would bring upon Ahaz and his kingdom by the Assyrians, notwithstanding their escape from this present storm, because they went on still in their wickedness, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.17-Isa.7.25">ver. 17-25</reference>. And this is written both for our comfort and for our admonition.
entries.d5caa14d5179fdf0f6ca8cb1f391c5ef617d9b9d: <div eID="gen15600" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15599" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Distress of Ahaz; Comfort Administered to Ahaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen15601" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, <hi type="italic">that</hi> Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up toward Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it was told the house of David, saying, Syria is confederate with Ephraim. And his heart was moved, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then said the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto Isaiah, Go forth now to meet Ahaz, thou, and Shear-jashub thy son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field; <hi type="super">4</hi> And say unto him, Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah. <hi type="super">5</hi> Because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have taken evil counsel against thee, saying, <hi type="super">6</hi> Let us go up against Judah, and vex it, and let us make a breach therein for us, and set a king in the midst of it, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the son of Tabeal: <hi type="super">7</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass. <hi type="super">8</hi> For the head of Syria <hi type="italic">is</hi> Damascus, and the head of Damascus <hi type="italic">is</hi> Rezin; and within threescore and five years shall Ephraim be broken, that it be not a people. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the head of Ephraim <hi type="italic">is</hi> Samaria, and the head of Samaria <hi type="italic">is</hi> Remaliah's son. If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established. <div eID="gen15601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15602" type="x-p"/> The prophet Isaiah had his commission renewed in the year that king Uzziah died, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1">ch. vi. 1</reference>. Jotham his son reigned, and reigned well, sixteen years. All that time, no doubt, Isaiah prophesied as he was commanded, and yet we have not in this book any of his prophecies dated in the reign of Jotham; but this, which is put first, was in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham. Many excellent useful sermons he preached which were not published and left upon record; for, if all that was memorable had been written, <hi type="italic">the world could not have contained the books,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.21.25">John xxi. 25</reference>. Perhaps in the reign of Ahaz, a wicked king, he had not opportunity to preach so much at court as in Jotham's time, and therefore then he wrote the more, for a testimony against them. Here is, <div eID="gen15602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15603" type="x-p"/> I. A very formidable design laid against Jerusalem by Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel, two neighbouring potentates, who had of late made descents upon Judah severally. At the end of the reign of Jotham, <hi type="italic">the Lord began to send against Judah Rezin and Pekah,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.37">2 Kings xv. 37</reference>. But now, in the second or third year of the reign of Ahaz, encouraged by their former successes, they entered into an alliance against Judah. Because Ahaz, though he found the sword over his head, began his reign with idolatry, <hi type="italic">God delivered him into the hand of the king of Syria and of the king of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.5">2 Chron. xxviii. 5</reference>), and a great slaughter they made in his kingdom, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.6-Isa.7.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Flushed with this victory, they went up towards Jerusalem, the royal city, to war against it, to besiege it, and make themselves masters of it; but it proved in the issue that they could not gain their point. Note, The sin of a land brings foreign invasions upon it and betrays the most advantageous posts and passes to the enemy; and God sometimes makes one wicked nation a scourge to another; but judgment, ordinarily, begins at the house of God. <div eID="gen15603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15604" type="x-p"/> II. The great distress that Ahaz and his court were in when they received advice of this design: <hi type="italic">It was told the house of David</hi> that Syria and Ephraim had signed a league against Judah, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.2">v. 2</reference>. This degenerate royal family is called the <hi type="italic">house of David,</hi> to put us in mind of that article of God's covenant with David (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.30-Ps.89.33">Ps. lxxxix. 30-33</reference>), <hi type="italic">If his children forsake my law, I will chasten their transgression with the rod; but my loving-kindness will I not utterly take away,</hi> which is remarkably fulfilled in this chapter. News being brought that the two armies of Syria and Israel were joined, and had taken the field, the court, the city, and the country, were thrown into consternation; <hi type="italic">The heart of Ahaz was moved with fear,</hi> and then no wonder that <hi type="italic">the heart of his people was so, as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind.</hi> They were tossed and shaken, and put into a great disorder and confusion, were wavering and uncertain in their counsels, hurried hither and thither, and could not fix in any steady resolution. They yielded to the storm, and gave up all for gone, concluding it in vain to make any resistance. Now that which caused this fright was the sense of guilt and the weakness of their faith. They had made God their enemy, and knew not how to make him their friend, and therefore their fears tyrannised over them; while those whose consciences are kept <hi type="italic">void of offence, and whose hearts are fixed, trusting in God, need not be afraid of evil tidings; though the earth be removed, yet will not they fear; but the wicked flee at the shaking of a leaf,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.36">Lev. xxvi. 36</reference>. <div eID="gen15604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15605" type="x-p"/> III. The orders and directions given to Isaiah to go and encourage Ahaz in his distress; not for his own sake (he deserved to hear nothing from God but words of terror, which might add affliction to his grief), but because he was a son of David and king of Judah. God had kindness for him for his father's sake, who must not be forgotten, and for his people's sake, who must not be abandoned, but would be encouraged if Ahaz were. Observe, <div eID="gen15605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15606" type="x-p"/> 1. God appointed the prophet to meet Ahaz, though he did not send to the prophet to speak with him, nor desire him to enquire of the Lord for him (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Go to meet Ahaz.</hi> Note, God is often found of those who seek him not, much more will he be found of those who seek him diligently. He speaks comfort to many who not only are not worthy of it, but do not so much as enquire after it. <div eID="gen15606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15607" type="x-p"/> 2. He ordered him to take his little son with him, because he carried a sermon in his name, <hi type="italic">Shear-jashub—A remnant shall return.</hi> The prophets sometimes recorded what they preached in the significant names of their children (as <reference osisRef="Hos.1.4">Hos. i. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.1.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.1.9">9</reference>); therefore Isaiah's children are said to be <hi type="italic">for signs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.18">ch. viii. 18</reference>. This son was so called for the encouragement of those of God's people who were carried captive, assuring them that they should return, at least a remnant of them, which was more than they could pretend to merit; yet at this time God was better than his word; for he took care not only that a remnant should return, but the whole number of those whom the confederate forces of Syria and Israel had taken prisoners, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.15">2 Chron. xxviii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen15607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15608" type="x-p"/> 3. He directed him where he should find Ahaz. He was to meet with him not in the temple, or the synagogue, or royal chapel, but <hi type="italic">at the end of the conduit of the upper pool,</hi> where he was, probably with many of his servants about him, contriving how to order the water-works, so as to secure them to the city, or deprive the enemy of the benefits of them (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.9-Isa.22.11">ch. xxii. 9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.3-2Chr.32.4">2 Chron. xxxii. 3, 4</reference>), or giving some necessary directions for the fortifying of the city as well as they could; and perhaps finding every thing in a bad posture or defence, the conduit out of repair, as well as other things gone to decay, his fears increased, and he was now in greater perplexity than ever; therefore, <hi type="italic">Go, meet him there.</hi> Note, God sometimes sends comforts to his people very seasonably, and, what time they are most afraid, encourages them to trust in him. <div eID="gen15608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15609" type="x-p"/> 4. He put words in his mouth, else the prophet would not have known how to bring a message of good to such a bad man, a sinner in Zion, that ought to be afraid; but God intended it for the support of faithful Israelites. <div eID="gen15609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15610" type="x-p"/> (1.) The prophet must rebuke their fears, and advise them by no means to yield to them, but keep their temper, and preserve the possession of their own souls (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Take heed, and be quiet.</hi> Note, In order to comfort there is need of caution; that we may be quiet, it is necessary that we take heed and watch against those things that threaten to disquiet us. "Fear not with this amazement, this fear, that weakens, and has torment; neither <hi type="italic">let thy heart be tender,</hi> so as to melt and fail within thee; but pluck up thy spirits, have a good heart on it, and be courageous; let not fear betray the succours which reason and religion offer for thy support." Note, Those who expect God should help them must help themselves, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.14">Ps. xxvii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen15610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15611" type="x-p"/> (2.) He must teach them to despise their enemies, not in pride, or security, or incogitancy (nothing more dangerous than so to despise an enemy), but in faith and dependence upon God. Ahaz's fear called them two powerful politic princes, for either of whom he was an unequal match, but, if united, he durst not look them in the face, nor make head against them. "No," says the prophet, "they are <hi type="italic">two tails of smoking firebrands;</hi> they are angry, they are fierce, they are furious, as firebrands, as fireballs; and they make one another worse by being in a confederacy, as sticks of fire put together burn the more violently. But they are only smoking firebrands: and where there is smoke there is some fire, but it may be not so much as was feared. Their threatenings will vanish into smoke. <hi type="italic">Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.17">Jer. xlvi. 17</reference>), and Rezin king of Syria but a smoke; and such are all the enemies of God's church, <hi type="italic">smoking flax,</hi> that will soon be quenched. Nay, they are but <hi type="italic">tails</hi> of smoking firebrands, in a manner burnt out already; their force is spent; they have consumed themselves with the heat of their own anger; you may put your foot on them, and tread them out." The two kingdoms of Syria and Israel were now near expiring. Note, The more we have an eye to God as a consuming fire the less reason we shall have to fear men, though they are ever so furious, nay, we shall be able to despise them as smoking firebrands. <div eID="gen15611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15612" type="x-p"/> (3.) He must assure them that the present design of these high allies (so they thought themselves) against Jerusalem should certainly be defeated and come to nothing, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.5-Isa.7.7">v. 5-7</reference>. [1.] That very thing which Ahaz thought most formidable is made the ground of their defeat—and that was the depth of their designs and the height of their hopes: "<hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> they shall be baffled and sent back with shame, <hi type="italic">because they have taken evil counsel against thee,</hi> which is an offence to God. These firebrands are a <hi type="italic">smoke in his nose</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">ch. lxv. 5</reference>), and therefore must be extinguished." <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They are very spiteful and malicious, and, therefore they shall not prosper. Judah had done them no wrong; they had no pretence to quarrel with Ahaz; but, without any reason, they said, <hi type="italic">Let us go up against Judah, and vex it.</hi> Note, Those that are vexatious cannot expect to be prosperous, those that love to do mischief cannot expect to do well. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They are very secure, and confident of success. They will vex Judah by going up against it; yet that is not all: they do not doubt but to make a breach in the wall of Jerusalem wide enough for them to march their army in at; or they count upon dissecting or dividing the kingdom into two parts, one for the king of Israel, the other for the king of Syria, who had agreed in one viceroy—<hi type="italic">a king</hi> to be <hi type="italic">set in the midst of it, even the son of Tabeal,</hi> some obscure person, it is uncertain whether a Syrian or an Israelite. So sure were they of gaining their point that they divided the prey before they had caught it. Note, Those that are most scornful are commonly least successful, for surely God scorns the scorners. [2.] God himself gives them his word that the attempt should not take effect (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord God,</hi> the sovereign Lord of all, who <hi type="italic">brings the counsel of the heathen to naught</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.10">Ps. xxxiii. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">It shall not stand, neither shall it come to pass;</hi> their measures shall all be broken, and they shall not be able to bring to pass their enterprise." Note, Whatever stands against God, or thinks to stand without him, cannot stand long. Man purposes, but God disposes; and <hi type="italic">who is he that saith and it cometh to pass if the Lord commands it not or countermands it?</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.37">Lam. iii. 37</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Prov.19.21">Prov. xix. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen15612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15613" type="x-p"/> (4.) He must give them a prospect of the destruction of these enemies, at last, that were now such a terror to them. [1.] They should neither of them enlarge their dominions, nor push their conquests any further; <hi type="italic">The head city of Syria is Damascus, and the head man of Damascus is Rezin;</hi> this he glories in, and this let him be content with, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">v. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">The head city of Ephraim</hi> has long been <hi type="italic">Samaria, and the head man in Samaria is</hi> now Pekah <hi type="italic">the son of Remaliah.</hi> These shall be made to know their own, their bounds are fixed, and they shall not pass them, to make themselves masters of the cities of Judah, much less to make Jerusalem their prey. Note, As God has appointed men the bounds of their habitation (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.26">Acts xvii. 26</reference>), so he has appointed princes the bounds of their dominion, within which they ought to confine themselves, and not encroach upon their neighbours' rights. [2.] Ephraim, which perhaps was the more malicious and forward enemy of the two, should shortly be quite rooted out, and should be so far from seizing other people's lands that they should not be able to hold their own. Interpreters are much at a loss how to compute the sixty-five years within which <hi type="italic">Ephraim shall cease to be a people;</hi> for the captivity of the ten tribes was but eleven years after this: and some make it a mistake of the transcriber, and think it should be read <hi type="italic">within six and five years,</hi> just eleven. But it is hard to allow that. Others make it to be sixty-five years from the time that the prophet Amos first foretold the ruin of the kingdom of the ten tribes; and some late interpreters make it to look as far forward as the last desolation of that country by Esarhaddon, which was about sixty-five years after this; then Ephraim was so broken that it was no more a people. Now it was the greatest folly in the world for those to be ruining their neighbours who were themselves marked for ruin, and so near to it. See what a prophet told them at this time, when they were triumphing over Judah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.10">2 Chron. xxviii. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Are there not with you, even with you, sins against the Lord your God?</hi> <div eID="gen15613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15614" type="x-p"/> (5.) He must urge them to mix faith with those assurances which he had given them (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If you will not believe</hi> what is said to you, <hi type="italic">surely you shall not be established;</hi> your shaken and disordered state shall not be established, your unquiet unsettled spirit shall not; though the things told you are very encouraging, yet they will not be so to you, unless you believe them, and be willing to take God's word." Note, The grace of faith is absolutely necessary to the quieting and composing of the mind in the midst of all the tosses of this present time, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.20">2 Chron. xx. 20</reference>.
entries.6cfeaa5fa84e25d18c0c5fd532df95d6c0d576a2: <div eID="gen15614" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Promise of Immanuel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen15615" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Moreover the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake again unto Ahaz, saying, <hi type="super">11</hi> Ask thee a sign of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above. <hi type="super">12</hi> But Ahaz said, I will not ask, neither will I tempt the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">13</hi> And he said, Hear ye now, O house of David; <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> a small thing for you to weary men, but will ye weary my God also? <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel. <hi type="super">15</hi> Butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good. <hi type="super">16</hi> For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land that thou abhorrest shall be forsaken of both her kings. <div eID="gen15615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15616" type="x-p"/> Here, I. God, by the prophet, makes a gracious offer to Ahaz, to confirm the foregoing predictions, and his faith in them, by such sign or miracle as he should choose (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.10-Isa.7.11">v. 10, 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ask thee a sign of the Lord thy God;</hi> See here the divine faithfulness and veracity. God tells us nothing but what he is able and ready to prove. See his wonderful condescension to the children of men, in that he is so <hi type="italic">willing to show to the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.17">Heb. vi. 17</reference>. He considers our frame, and that, living in a world of sense, we are apt to require sensible proofs, which therefore he has favoured us with in sacramental signs and seals. Ahaz was a bad man, yet God is called the Lord his God, because he was a child of Abraham and David, and of the covenants made with them. See how gracious God is even to the evil and unthankful; Ahaz is bidden to choose his sign, as Gideon about the fleece (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.37">Judg. vi. 37</reference>); let him ask for a sign in the air, or earth, or water, for God's power is the same in all. <div eID="gen15616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15617" type="x-p"/> II. Ahaz rudely refuses this gracious offer, and (which is not mannerly towards any superior) kicks at the courtesy, and puts a slight upon it (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will not ask.</hi> The true reason why he would not ask for a sign was because, having a dependence upon the Assyrians, their forces, and their gods, for help, he would not thus far be beholden to the God of Israel, or lay himself under obligations to him. He would not ask a sign for the confirming of his faith because he resolved to persist in his unbelief, and would indulge his doubts and distrusts; yet he pretends a pious reason: <hi type="italic">I will not tempt the Lord;</hi> as if it would be a tempting of God to do that which God himself invited and directed him to do. Note, A secret disaffection to God is often disguised with the specious colours of respect to him; and those who are resolved that they will not trust God yet pretend that they will not tempt him. <div eID="gen15617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15618" type="x-p"/> III. The prophet reproves him and his court, him and the house of David, the whole royal family, for their contempt of prophecy, and the little value they had for divine revelation (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.13">v. 13</reference>) "<hi type="italic">Is it a small thing for you to weary men</hi> by your oppression and tyranny, with which you make yourselves burdensome and odious to all mankind? But <hi type="italic">will you weary my God also</hi> with the affronts you put upon him?" As the unjust judge that neither <hi type="italic">feared God nor regarded man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.18.2">Luke xviii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">You have wearied the Lord with your words,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.17">Mal. ii. 17</reference>. Nothing is more grievous to the God of heaven than to be distrusted. "<hi type="italic">Will you weary my God?</hi> Will you suppose him to be tired and unable to help you, or to be weary of doing you good? Whereas <hi type="italic">the youths may faint and be weary,</hi> you may have tired all your friends, <hi type="italic">the Creator of the ends of the earth faints not, neither is weary.</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.40.28-Isa.40.31">ch. xl. 28-31</reference>. Or this: "In affronting the prophets, you think you put a slight only upon men like yourselves, and consider not that you affront God himself, whose messengers they are, and put a slight upon him, who will resent it accordingly." The prophet here calls God his God with a great deal of pleasure: Ahaz would not say, He is my God, though the prophet had invited him to say so (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord thy God;</hi> but Isaiah will say, "He is mine." Note, Whatever others do, we must avouch the Lord for ours and abide by him. <div eID="gen15618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15619" type="x-p"/> IV. The prophet, in God's name, gives them a sign: "You will not ask a sign, but the unbelief of man shall not make the promise of God of no effect: <hi type="italic">The Lord himself shall give you a sign</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">v. 14</reference>), a double sign." <div eID="gen15619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15620" type="x-p"/> 1. "A sign in general of his good-will to Israel and to the house of David. You may conclude it that he has mercy in store for you, and that you are not forsaken of your God, how great soever your present distress and danger are; for of your nation, of your family, the Messiah is to be born, and you cannot be destroyed while that blessing is in you, which shall be introduced," (1.) "In a glorious manner; for, whereas you have been often told that he should be born among you, I am now further to tell you that he shall be born of a virgin, which will signify both the divine power and the divine purity with which he shall be brought into the world,—that he shall be a extraordinary person, for he shall not be born by ordinary generation,—and that he shall be a holy thing, not stained with the common pollutions of the human nature, therefore incontestably fit to have the throne of his father David given him." Now this, though it was to be accomplished above 500 years after, was a most encouraging sign to the house of David (and to them, under that title, this prophecy is directed, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.13">v. 13</reference>) and an assurance that God would not cast them off. Ephraim did indeed envy Judah (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.13">ch. xi. 13</reference>) and sought the ruin of that kingdom, but could not prevail; for the sceptre should never depart from Judah till the coming of Shiloh, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>. Those whom God designs for the great salvation may take that for a sign to them that they shall not be swallowed up by any trouble they meet with in the way. (2.) The Messiah shall be introduced on a glorious errand, wrapped up in his glorious name: They <hi type="italic">shall call his name Immanuel—God with us,</hi> God in our nature, God at peace with us, in covenant with us. This was fulfilled in their calling him <hi type="italic">Jesus—a Saviour</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.21-Matt.1.25">Matt. i. 21-25</reference>), for, if he had not been <hi type="italic">Immanuel—God with us,</hi> he could not have been <hi type="italic">Jesus—a Saviour.</hi> Now this was a further sign of God's favour to the house of David and the tribe of Judah; for he that intended to work this great salvation among them no doubt would work out for them all those other salvations which were to be the types and figures of this, and as it were preludes to this. "Here is a sign for you, not in the depth nor in the height, but in the prophecy, in the promise, in the covenant made with David, which you are no strangers to. The promised seed shall be Immanuel, <hi type="italic">God with us;</hi> let that word comfort you (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.10">ch. viii. 10</reference>), that <hi type="italic">God is with us,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">v. 8</reference>) that your land is Immanuel's land. Let not <hi type="italic">the heart of the house of David</hi> be moved thus (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.2">v. 2</reference>), nor let Judah fear the setting up of the son of Tabeal (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.6">v. 6</reference>), for nothing can cut off the entail on the Son of David that shall be Immanuel." Note, The strongest consolations, in time of trouble, are those which are borrowed from Christ, our relation to him, our interest in him, and our expectations of him and from him. Of this child it is further foretold (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.15">v. 15</reference>) that though he shall not be born like other children, but of a virgin, yet he shall be really and truly man, and shall be nursed and brought up like other children: <hi type="italic">Butter and honey shall he eat,</hi> as other children do, particularly the children of that land which <hi type="italic">flowed with milk and honey.</hi> Though he be conceived by the power of the Holy Ghost, yet he shall not therefore be fed with angels' food, but, as it becomes him, shall be <hi type="italic">in all things made like unto his brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.17">Heb. ii. 17</reference>. Nor shall he, though born thus by extraordinary generation, be a man immediately, but, as other children, shall advance gradually through the several states of infancy, childhood, and youth, to that of manhood, and growing in wisdom and stature, shall at length wax strong in spirit, and come to maturity, so as to know how <hi type="italic">to refuse the evil and choose the good.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Luke.2.40">Luke ii. 40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.52">52</reference>. Note, Children are fed when they are little that they may be taught and instructed when they have grown up; they have their maintenance in order to their education. <div eID="gen15620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15621" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is another sign in particular of the speedy destruction of these potent princes that were now a terror to Judah, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.16">v. 16</reference>. "Before <hi type="italic">this</hi> child (so it should be read), this child which I have now in my arms" (he means not Immanuel, but Shear-jashub his own son, whom he was ordered to take with him for a sign, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">v. 3</reference>), "before this <hi type="italic">child shall know how to refuse the evil and choose the good</hi>" (and those who saw what his present stature and forwardness were would easily conjecture how long that would be), "before this child be three or four years older, <hi type="italic">the land that thou abhorrest,</hi> these confederate forces of Israelites and Syrians, which thou hast such an enmity to and standest in such dread of, <hi type="italic">shall be forsaken of both their kings,</hi> both Pekah and Rezin," who were in so close an alliance that they seemed as if they were the kings of but one kingdom. This was fully accomplished; for within two or three years after this, Hoshea conspired against Pekah, and slew him (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.30">2 Kings xv. 30</reference>), and, before that, the king of Assyria took Damascus, and slew Rezin, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2 Kings xvi. 9</reference>. Nay, there was a present event, which happened immediately, and when this child carried the prediction of in his name, which was a pledge and earnest of this future event. <hi type="italic">Shear-jashub</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">The remnant shall return,</hi> which doubtless points at the wonderful return of those 200,000 captives whom Pekah and Rezin had carried away, who were brought back, not by might or power, but by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts. Read the story, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.8-2Chr.28.15">2 Chron. xxviii. 8-15</reference>. The prophetical naming of this child having thus had its accomplishment, no doubt this, which was further added concerning him, should have its accomplishment likewise, that Syria and Israel should be deprived of both their kings. One mercy from God encourages us to hope for another, if it engages us to prepare for another.
entries.0fed59057b8db44959c72c07c2d03ecf760720f5: <div eID="gen15621" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments Announced. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 740.)</title> <div sID="gen15622" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall bring upon thee, and upon thy people, and upon thy father's house, days that have not come, from the day that Ephraim departed from Judah; <hi type="italic">even</hi> the king of Assyria. <hi type="super">18</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall hiss for the fly that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the land of Assyria. <hi type="super">19</hi> And they shall come, and shall rest all of them in the desolate valleys, and in the holes of the rocks, and upon all thorns, and upon all bushes. <hi type="super">20</hi> In the same day shall the Lord shave with a razor that is hired, <hi type="italic">namely,</hi> by them beyond the river, by the king of Assyria, the head, and the hair of the feet: and it shall also consume the beard. <hi type="super">21</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> a man shall nourish a young cow, and two sheep; <hi type="super">22</hi> And it shall come to pass, for the abundance of milk <hi type="italic">that</hi> they shall give he shall eat butter: for butter and honey shall every one eat that is left in the land. <hi type="super">23</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, <hi type="italic">that</hi> every place shall be, where there were a thousand vines at a thousand silverlings, it shall <hi type="italic">even</hi> be for briers and thorns. <hi type="super">24</hi> With arrows and with bows shall <hi type="italic">men</hi> come thither; because all the land shall become briers and thorns. <hi type="super">25</hi> And <hi type="italic">on</hi> all hills that shall be digged with the mattock, there shall not come thither the fear of briers and thorns: but it shall be for the sending forth of oxen, and for the treading of lesser cattle. <div eID="gen15622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15623" type="x-p"/> After the comfortable promises made to Ahaz as a branch of the house of David, here follow terrible threatenings against him, as a degenerate branch of that house; for though the loving-kindness of God shall not be utterly taken away, for the sake of David and the covenant made with him, yet his iniquity shall be <hi type="italic">chastened with the rod,</hi> and his sin with stripes. Let those that will not mix faith with the promises of God expect to hear the alarms of his threatenings. <div eID="gen15623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15624" type="x-p"/> I. The judgment threatened is very great, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.17">v. 17</reference>. It is very great, for it is general; it shall be brought upon the prince himself (high as he is, he shall not be out of the reach of it), and upon the people, the whole body of the nation, and upon the royal family, <hi type="italic">upon</hi> all <hi type="italic">thy father's house;</hi> it shall be a judgment entailed on posterity, and shall go along with the royal blood. It is very great, for it shall be unprecedented—<hi type="italic">days that have not come;</hi> so dark, so gloomy, so melancholy, as never were the like since the revolt of the ten tribes, when Ephraim departed from Judah, which was indeed a sad time to the house of David. Note, The longer men continue in sin the sorer punishments they have reason to expect. It is the Lord that will bring these days upon them, for our times are in his hand, and who can resist or escape the judgments he brings? <div eID="gen15624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15625" type="x-p"/> II. The enemy that should be employed as the instrument of this judgment is the king of Assyria. Ahaz reposed great confidence in that prince for help against the confederate powers of Israel and Syria, and minded the less what God said to him by his prophet for his encouragement because he built much upon his interest in the king of Assyria, and had meanly promised to be his servant if he would send him some succours; he had also, made him a present of gold and silver, for which he drained the treasures both of church and state, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7-2Kgs.16.8">2 Kings xvi. 7, 8</reference>. Now God threatens that that king of Assyria whom he made his stay instead of God should become a scourge to him. He was so speedily; for, when he <hi type="italic">came to him, he distressed him, but strengthened him not</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.20">2 Chron. xxviii. 20</reference>), the reed not only broke under him, but ran into his hand, and pierced it, and thenceforward the kings of Assyria were, for a long time, grieving thorns to Judah, and gave them a great deal of trouble. Note, The creature that we make our hope commonly proves our hurt. The king of Assyria, not long after this, made himself master of the ten tribes, carried them captive, and laid their country waste, so as fully to answer the prediction here; and perhaps it may refer to that, as an explication of <reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">v. 8</reference>, where it is foretold that Ephraim shall be broken, that it shall not be a people; and it is easy to suppose that the prophet (at <reference osisRef="Isa.7.17">v. 17</reference>) turns his speech to the king of Israel, denouncing God's judgments against him for invading Judah. But the expositors universally understand it of Ahaz and his kingdom. Now observe, 1. Summons given to the invaders (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord shall whistle for the fly and the bee.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">ch. v. 26</reference>. Enemies that seem as contemptible as a fly or a bee, and are as easily crushed, shall yet, when God pleases, do his work as effectually as lions and young lions. Though they are as far distant from one another as the rivers of Egypt and the land of Assyria, yet they shall punctually meet to join in this work when God commands their attendance; for, when God has work to do, he will not be at a loss for instruments to do it with. 2. Possession taken by them, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.19">v. 19</reference>. It should seem as if the country were in no condition to make resistance. They find no difficulties in forcing their way, but <hi type="italic">come and rest all of them in the desolate valleys,</hi> which the inhabitants had deserted upon the first alarm, and left them a cheap and easy prey to the invaders. They shall come and rest in the low grounds like swarms of flies and bees, and shall render themselves impregnable by taking shelter in the holes of the rocks, as bees often do, and showing themselves formidable by appearing openly upon all thorns and all bushes; so generally shall the land be overspread with them. These bees shall knit upon the thorns and bushes, and there rest undisturbed. 3. Great desolations made, and the country generally depopulated (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord shall shave the hair of the head, and beard, and feet;</hi> he shall sweep all away, as the leper, when he was cleansed, <hi type="italic">shaved off all his hair,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.14.8-Lev.14.9">Lev. xiv. 8, 9</reference>. This is done with a razor which is hired, either which God has hired (as if he had none of his own; but what he hires, and whom he employs in any service for him, he will pay for. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.18-Ezek.29.19">Ezek. xxix. 18, 19</reference>), or which Ahaz has hired for his assistance. God will make that to be an instrument of his destruction which he hired into his service. Note, Many are beaten with that arm of flesh which they trusted to rather than to the arm of the Lord, and which they were at a great expense upon, when by faith and prayer they might have found cheap and easy succour in God. 4. The consequences of this general depopulation. (1.) The flocks of cattle shall be all destroyed, so that a man who had herds and flocks in abundance shall be stripped of them all by the enemy, and shall with much ado save for his own use a young cow and two sheep—a poor stock (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.21">v. 21</reference>), yet he shall think himself happy in having any left. (2.) The few cattle that are left shall have such a large compass of ground to feed in that <hi type="italic">they shall give abundance of milk,</hi> and very good milk, such as shall produce butter enough, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.22">v. 22</reference>. There shall also be such want of men that the milk of one cow and two sheep shall serve a whole family, which used to keep abundance of servants and consume a great deal, but is now reduced. (3.) The breed of cattle shall be destroyed; so that those who used to eat flesh ( as the Jews commonly did) shall be necessitated to confine themselves to butter and honey, for there shall be no flesh for them; and the country shall be so depopulated that there shall be butter and honey enough for the few that are left in it. (4.) Good land, that used to be let well, shall be all overrun with briers and thorns (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.23">v. 23</reference>); where there used to be a thousand vines planted, for which the tenants used to pay a thousand shekels, or pieces of silver, yearly rent, there shall be nothing now but briers and thorns, no profit either for landlord or tenant, all being laid waste by the army of the invaders. Note, God can soon turn a fruitful land into barrenness; and it is just with him to turn vines into briers if we, instead of bringing forth grapes to him, bring forth wild grapes, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">ch. v. 4</reference>. (5.) The implements of husbandry shall be turned into instruments of war, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.24">v. 24</reference>. The whole land having become briers and thorns, the grounds that men used to come to with sickles and pruning-hooks to gather in the fruits they shall now come to with arrows and bows, to hunt for wild beasts in the thickets, or to defend themselves from the robbers that lurk in the bushes, seeking for prey, or to kill the serpents and venomous beasts that are hid there. This denotes a very sad change of the face of that pleasant land. But what melancholy change is there which sin will not make with a people? (6.) Where briers and thorns were wont to be of use and to do good service, even in the hedges, for the defence of the enclosed grounds, they shall be plucked up, and all laid in common. There shall be briers and thorns in abundance where they should not be, but none where they should be, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.25">v. 25</reference>. <hi type="italic">The hills that shall be digged with the mattock,</hi> for special use, from which the cattle used to be kept off with the fear of briers and thorns, shall now be thrown open, the <hi type="italic">hedges broken down for the boar out of the wood</hi> to waste it, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.12-Ps.80.13">Ps. lxxx. 12, 13</reference>. It shall be left at large for oxen to run in and less cattle. See the effect of sin and the curse; it has made the earth a forest of thorns and thistles, except as it is forced into some order by the constant care and labour of man. And see what folly it is to set our hearts upon possessions of lands, be they every so fruitful, ever so pleasant; if they lie ever so little neglected and uncultivated, or if they be abused by a wasteful careless heir or tenant, or the country be laid waste by war, they will soon become frightful deserts. Heaven is a paradise not subject to such changes.  <chapter eID="Isa.7"/> <div eID="gen15625" type="x-p"/>

entries.6ea7c66b4e1de9f102d6c800944f848bc0e328f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8431"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <div sID="gen13578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Is 7:<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1-9:7</reference>. Prediction of the Ill Success of the Syro- Israelitish Invasion of Judah--</hi>Ahaz's Alliance with Assyria, and Its Fatal Results to Judea--Yet the Certainty of Final Preservation and of the Coming of Messiah.<div eID="gen13578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13579" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">In the Assyrian inscriptions the name of Rezin, king of Damascus, is found among the tributaries of Tiglath-pileser, of whose reign the annals of seventeen years have been deciphered. For the historical facts in this chapter, compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.37-2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 15:37-16:9</reference>. Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel, as confederates, advanced against Jerusalem. In the first campaign they "smote Ahaz with a great slaughter" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.5">2Ch 28:5</reference>). Their object was probably to unite the three kingdoms against Assyria. Egypt seems to have favored the plan, so as to interpose these confederate kingdoms between her own frontier and Assyria (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Is 7:18</reference>, "Egypt"; and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>, Hoshea's league with Egypt). Rezin and Pekah may have perceived Ahaz' inclination towards Assyria rather than towards their own confederacy; this and the old feud between Israel and Judah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.16">1Ki 12:16</reference>) occasioned their invasion of Judah. Ahaz, at the second inroad of his enemies (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.1-2Chr.28.26">2Ch 28:1-26</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.37">2Ki 15:37</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.16.5">Is 16:5</reference>), smarting under his former defeat, applied to Tiglath-pileser, in spite of Isaiah's warning in this chapter, that he should rather rely on God; that king accordingly attacked Damascus, and slew Rezin (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>); and probably it was at the same time that he carried away part of Israel captive (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>), unless there were two assaults on Pekah--</hi>that in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>, the earlier, and that in which Tiglath helped Ahaz subsequently [G. V. Smith]. Ahaz was saved at the sacrifice of Judah's independence and the payment of a large tribute, which continued till the overthrow of Sennacherib under Hezekiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.37">Is 37:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.8">2Ki 16:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.18">17, 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.20">2Ch 28:20</reference>). Ahaz' reign began about 741 B.C., and Pekah was slain in 738 [Winer].<div eID="gen13579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8431"/><hi type="bold">1. Ahaz--</hi>In the first years of his reign the design of the two kings against Judah was carried out, which was formed in Jotham's reign (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.37">2Ki 15:37</reference>).<div eID="gen13580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13581" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Syria--</hi>Hebrew, Aram (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Ge 10:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.23">23</reference>), originally the whole region between the Euphrates and Mediterranean, including Assyria, of which Syria is an abbreviation; here the region round Damascus, and along Mount Libanus.<div eID="gen13581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem--</hi>An actual siege of it took place, but was foiled (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.5">2Ki 16:5</reference>). <div eID="gen13582" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec833f2a8111283580c3f36a8ff98effcfe31373: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8432"/><div sID="gen13583" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8432"/><hi type="bold">2. is confederate with--</hi>rather, is encamped upon the territory of Ephraim [Maurer], or better, as Rezin was encamped against Jerusalem, "is supported by" [Lowth] Ephraim, whose land lay between Syria and Judah. The mention of "David" alludes, in sad contrast with the present, to the time when David made Syria subject to him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.6">2Sa 8:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ephraim--</hi>the ten tribes.<div eID="gen13584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ... trees of ... wood--</hi>a simultaneous agitation. <div eID="gen13585" type="x-p"/>
entries.76cf495b62db9978c68e822f16abdc9dc2133686: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8433"/><div sID="gen13586" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8433"/><hi type="bold">3. Go forth--</hi>out of the city, to the place where Ahaz was superintending the works for defense and the cutting off of the water supply from the enemy, and securing it to the city. So <reference osisRef="Isa.22.9">Is 22:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.4">2Ch 32:4</reference>.<div eID="gen13586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shearjashub--</hi>that is, A remnant shall return (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.13">Is 6:13</reference>). His very name (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Is 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.3">Is 8:3</reference>) was a standing memorial to Ahaz and the Jews that the nation should not, notwithstanding the general calamity (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.17-Isa.7.25">Is 7:17-25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.6-Isa.8.8">Is 8:6-8</reference>), be utterly destroyed (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.21">Is 10:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen13587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">conduit--</hi>an aqueduct from the pool or reservoir for the supply of the city. At the foot of Zion was Fount Siloah (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Is 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.15">Ne 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.9.7">Joh 9:7</reference>), called also Gihon, on the west of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.30">2Ch 32:30</reference>). Two pools were supplied from it, the Upper, or Old (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Is 22:11</reference>), or King's (<reference osisRef="Neh.2.14">Ne 2:14</reference>), and the Lower (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.9">Is 22:9</reference>), which received the superfluous waters of the upper. The upper pool is still to be seen, about seven hundred yards from the Jaffa gate. The highway leading to the fullers' field, which was in a position near water for the purposes of washing, previous to drying and bleaching, the cloth, was probably alongside the aqueduct. <div eID="gen13588" type="x-p"/>
entries.addb4539be10b7cee4b63d7a82eb24dd1cfb65ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8434"/><div sID="gen13589" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8434"/><hi type="bold">4. Take heed, &c.--</hi>that is, See that thou be quiet (not seeking Assyrian aid in a fit of panic).<div eID="gen13589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tails--</hi>mere ends of firebrands, almost consumed themselves (about soon to fall before the Assyrians, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">Is 7:8</reference>), therefore harmless.<div eID="gen13590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13591" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smoking--</hi>as about to go out; not blazing.<div eID="gen13591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Remaliah--</hi>Pekah, a usurper (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.25">2Ki 15:25</reference>). The Easterners express contempt by designating one, not by his own name, but by his father's, especially when the father is but little known (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.27">1Sa 20:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.31">31</reference>). <div eID="gen13592" type="x-p"/>
entries.3fd99936033360359269ed086d8ff7fce2bb8f3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8435"/><div sID="gen13593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8435"/><hi type="bold">6. vex--</hi>rather, "throw into consternation" [Gesenius].<div eID="gen13593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make a breach--</hi>rather, "cleave it asunder." Their scheme was to divide a large portion of the territory between themselves, and set up a vassal king of their own over the rest.<div eID="gen13594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Tabeal--</hi>unknown; a Syrian-sounding name, perhaps favored by a party in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.6">Is 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">9, 12</reference>). <div eID="gen13595" type="x-p"/>
entries.58a5785d27c66e6885c437ecbf96b755b0bbca94: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8436"/><div sID="gen13596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8436"/>7. (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.10">Is 8:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.30">Pr 21:30</reference>). <div eID="gen13596" type="x-p"/>
entries.91025e4ce50937a7be6107ed6362c9ae7ffe80d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8437"/><div sID="gen13597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8437"/><hi type="bold">8. head--</hi>that is, in both Syria and Israel the capital shall remain as it is; they shall not conquer Judah, but each shall possess only his own dominions.<div eID="gen13597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">threescore and five ... not a people--</hi>As these words break the symmetry of the parallelism in this verse, either they ought to be placed after "Remaliah's son," in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.9">Is 7:9</reference>, or else they refer to some older prophecy of Isaiah, or of Amos (as the Jewish writers represent), parenthetically; to which, in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.8">Is 7:8</reference>, the words, "If ye will not believe ... not be established," correspond in parallelism. One deportation of Israel happened within one or two years from this time, under Tiglath-pileser (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>). Another in the reign of Hoshea, under Shalmaneser (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.1-2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:1-6</reference>), was about twenty years after. But the final one which utterly "broke" up Israel so as to be "not a people," accompanied by a colonization of Samaria with foreigners, was under Esar-haddon, who carried away Manasseh, king of Judah, also, in the twenty-second year of his reign, sixty-five years from the utterance of this prophecy (compare <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.2">Ezr 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.10">3, 10</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.24">2Ki 17:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.11">2Ch 33:11</reference>) [Usher]. The event, though so far off, was enough to assure the people of Judah that as God, the Head of the theocracy, would ultimately interpose to destroy the enemies of His people, so they might rely on Him now. <div eID="gen13598" type="x-p"/>
entries.15ac05661894fa1f343c68978e4be4a11180bb30: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8438"/><div sID="gen13599" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8438"/><hi type="bold">9. believe, ... be established--</hi>There is a paronomasia, or play on the words, in the Hebrew: "if ye will not confide, ye shall not abide." Ahaz brought distress on himself by distrust in the Lord, and trust in Assyria. <div eID="gen13599" type="x-p"/>
entries.6991ff5512f4be62438729b94b1148f4a74fbd1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8439"/><div sID="gen13600" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8439"/><hi type="bold">11. Ask thee--</hi>since thou dost not credit the prophet's words.<div eID="gen13600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13601" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sign--</hi>a miraculous token to assure thee that God will fulfil His promise of saving Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.30">Is 37:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.38.7">38:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.8">8</reference>). "Signs," facts then present or near at hand as pledges for the more distant future, are frequent in Isaiah.<div eID="gen13601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13602" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ask ... in ... depth--</hi>literally, "Make deep ... ask it," that is, Go to the depth of the earth or of Hades [Vulgate and Lowth], or, Mount high for it (literally, "Make high"). So in <reference osisRef="Matt.16.1">Mt 16:1</reference>. Signs in heaven are contrasted with the signs on earth and below it (raising the dead) which Jesus Christ had wrought (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.10.6">Ro 10:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.7">7</reference>). He offers Ahaz the widest limits within which to make his choice. <div eID="gen13602" type="x-p"/>
entries.21ce53ad08aec4dd65552f84c8ea6d7519a36926: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8440"/><div sID="gen13603" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8440"/><hi type="bold">12. neither ... tempt--</hi>hypocritical pretext of keeping the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.16">De 6:16</reference>); "tempt," that is, put God to the proof, as in <reference osisRef="Matt.4.7">Mt 4:7</reference>, by seeking His miraculous interposition without warrant. But here there was the warrant of the prophet of God; to have asked a sign, when thus offered, would not have been a tempting of God. Ahaz' true reason for declining was his resolve not to do God's will, but to negotiate with Assyria, and persevere in his idolatry (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7">2Ki 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.3">8, 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.10">4, 10</reference>). Men often excuse their distrust in God, and trust in their own devices, by professed reverence for God. Ahaz may have fancied that though Jehovah was the God of Judea and could work a sign there, that was no proof that the local god of Syria might not be more powerful. Such was the common heathen notion (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.10">Is 10:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.36.18-Isa.36.20">36:18-20</reference>). <div eID="gen13603" type="x-p"/>
entries.20e6fe0e53f83ee27d4a4a9ed58f3a72dfe4f63e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8441"/><div sID="gen13604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8441"/><hi type="bold">13. Is it a small thing?--</hi>Is it not enough for you (<reference osisRef="Num.16.9">Nu 16:9</reference>)? The allusion to "David" is in order to contrast his trust in God with his degenerate descendant Ahaz' distrust.<div eID="gen13604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weary--</hi>try the patience of.<div eID="gen13605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">men--</hi>prophets. Isaiah as yet had given no outward proof that he was from God; but now God has offered a sign, which Ahaz publicly rejects. The sin is therefore now not merely against "men," but openly against "God." Isaiah's manner therefore changes from mildness to bold reproof. <div eID="gen13606" type="x-p"/>
entries.aeb1786e7d6076e2016d78badc8d67463cc8a990: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8442"/><div sID="gen13607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8442"/><hi type="bold">14. himself--</hi>since thou wilt not ask a sign, nay, rejectest the offer of one.<div eID="gen13607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">you--</hi>for the sake of the house of believing "David" (God remembering His everlasting covenant with David), not for unbelieving Ahaz' sake.<div eID="gen13608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Behold--</hi>arresting attention to the extraordinary prophecy.<div eID="gen13609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">virgin--</hi>from a root, "to lie hid," virgins being closely kept from men's gaze in their parents' custody in the East. The Hebrew, and the Septuagint here, and Greek (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.23">Mt 1:23</reference>), have the article, the virgin, some definite one known to the speaker and his hearers; primarily, the woman, then a virgin, about immediately to become the second wife, and bear a child, whose attainment of the age of discrimination (about three years) should be preceded by the deliverance of Judah from its two invaders; its fullest significancy is realized in "the woman" (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Ge 3:15</reference>), whose seed should bruise the serpent's head and deliver captive man (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.22">Jr 31:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.3">Mi 5:3</reference>). Language is selected such as, while partially applicable to the immediate event, receives its fullest, most appropriate, and exhaustive accomplishment in Messianic events. The New Testament application of such prophecies is not a strained "accommodation"; rather the temporary fulfilment of an adaptation of the far-reaching prophecy to the present passing event, which foreshadows typically the great central end of prophecy, Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.10">Re 19:10</reference>). Evidently the wording is such as to apply more fully to Jesus Christ than to the prophet's son; "virgin" applies, in its simplest sense, to the Virgin Mary, rather than to the prophetess who ceased to be a virgin when she "conceived"; "Immanuel," God with us (<reference osisRef="John.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>), cannot in a strict sense apply to Isaiah's son, but only to Him who is presently called expressly (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>), "the Child, the Son, Wonderful (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.8.18">Is 8:18</reference>), the mighty God." Local and temporary features (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.15">Is 7:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.16">16</reference>) are added in every type; otherwise it would be no type, but the thing itself. There are resemblances to the great Antitype sufficient to be recognized by those who seek them; dissimilarities enough to confound those who do not desire to discover them.<div eID="gen13610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call--</hi>that is, "she shall," or as Margin, "thou, O Virgin, shalt call;" mothers often named their children (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.1">Ge 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.19.37">19:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.29.32">29:32</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Matt.1.23">Mt 1:23</reference> the expression is strikingly changed into, "They shall call"; when the prophecy received its full accomplishment, no longer is the name Immanuel restricted to the prophetess' view of His character, as in its partial fulfilment in her son; all shall then call (that is, not literally), or regard Him as peculiarly and most fitly characterized by the descriptive name, "Immanuel" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.9">Col 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen13611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name--</hi>not mere appellation, which neither Isaiah's son nor Jesus Christ bore literally; but what describes His manifested attributes; His character (so <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>). The name in its proper destination was not arbitrary, but characteristic of the individual; sin destroyed the faculty of perceiving the internal being; hence the severance now between the name and the character; in the case of Jesus Christ and many in Scripture, the Holy Ghost has supplied this want [Olshausen]. <div eID="gen13612" type="x-p"/>
entries.d06e25aa14317a64aa4ec9cc1ca416a9e7bb4d39: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8443"/><div sID="gen13613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8443"/><hi type="bold">15. Butter--</hi>rather, curdled milk, the acid of which is grateful in the heat of the East (<reference osisRef="Job.20.17">Job 20:17</reference>).<div eID="gen13613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honey--</hi>abundant in Palestine (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.8">Jud 14:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.25">1Sa 14:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.3.4">Mt 3:4</reference>). Physicians directed that the first food given to a child should be honey, the next milk [Barnabas, Epistle]. Horsley takes this as implying the real humanity of the Immanuel Jesus Christ, about to be fed as other infants (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.52">Lu 2:52</reference>). <reference osisRef="Isa.7.22">Is 7:22</reference> shows that besides the fitness of milk and honey for children, a state of distress of the inhabitants is also implied, when, by reason of the invaders, milk and honey, things produced spontaneously, shall be the only abundant articles of food [Maurer].<div eID="gen13614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13615" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he may know--</hi>rather, until He shall know.<div eID="gen13615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil ... choose ... good--</hi>At about three years of age moral consciousness begins (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.8.4">Is 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.1.39">De 1:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.4.11">Jon 4:11</reference>). <div eID="gen13616" type="x-p"/>
entries.4df8589224f47fc2021afdb25543f6ac72c84b48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8444"/><div sID="gen13617" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8444"/><hi type="bold">16. For--</hi>The deliverance implied in the name "Immanuel," and the cessation of distress as to food (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Is 7:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.15">15</reference>), shall last only till the child grows to know good and evil;<div eID="gen13617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ... the land that ... abhorrest ... forsaken of ... kings--</hi>rather, desolate shall be the land, before whose two kings thou art alarmed [Hengstenberg and Gesenius].<div eID="gen13618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the land--</hi>namely, Syria and Samaria regarded as one (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.30">15:30</reference>), just two years after this prophecy, as it foretells. Horsley takes it, "The land (Judah and Samaria) of (the former of) which thou art the plague (literally, 'thorn') shall be forsaken," &c.; a prediction thus, that Judah and Israel (appropriately regarded as one "land") should cease to be kingdoms (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.1">Lu 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Ge 49:10</reference>) before Immanuel came.<div eID="gen13619" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.7.17-Isa.7.25">Is 7:17-25</reference>. Fatal Consequences of Ahaz' Assyrian Policy.</title> <div sID="gen13620" type="x-p"/> Though temporary deliverance (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.16">Is 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.4">8:4</reference>) was to be given then, and final deliverance through Messiah, sore punishment shall follow the former. After subduing Syria and Israel, the Assyrians shall encounter Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>), and Judah shall be the battlefield of both (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Is 7:18</reference>), and be made tributary to that very Assyria (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.20">2Ch 28:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7">2Ki 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.8">8</reference>) now about to be called in as an ally (<reference osisRef="Isa.39.1-Isa.39.6">Is 39:1-6</reference>). Egypt, too, should prove a fatal ally (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.6">Is 36:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">31:1</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen13620" type="x-p"/>
entries.a388ecafd7525481f8be2f87c94dd6dbe91c5b40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8445"/><div sID="gen13621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8445"/><hi type="bold">18. hiss--</hi>whistle, to bring bees to settle (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.5.26">Is 5:26</reference>).<div eID="gen13621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fly--</hi>found in numbers about the arms of the Nile and the canals from it (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.5-Isa.7.23">Is 19:5-7; 23</reference>:<reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">3</reference>), here called "rivers." Hence arose the plague of flies (<reference osisRef="Exod.8.21">Ex 8:21</reference>). Figurative, for numerous and troublesome foes from the remotest parts of Egypt, for example, Pharaoh-nechoh.<div eID="gen13622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.1.44">De 1:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.12">Psa 118:12</reference>). As numerous in Assyria as the fly in marshy Egypt. Sennacherib, Esar-haddon, and Nebuchadnezzar fulfilled this prediction. <div eID="gen13623" type="x-p"/>
entries.afff2b4d149ded276ea27f954f562d400ea7498b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8446"/><div sID="gen13624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8446"/><hi type="bold">19. rest--</hi>image of flies and bees kept up. The enemy shall overspread the land everywhere, even in "desolate valleys."<div eID="gen13624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thorns--</hi>wild, contrasted with "bushes," which were valued and objects of care (see Margin). <div eID="gen13625" type="x-p"/>
entries.80c502034b377d8de1b98b497e3eb121ade3dc6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8447"/><div sID="gen13626" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8447"/><hi type="bold">20. razor--</hi>The Assyrians are to be God's instrument of devastating Judea, just as a razor sweeps away all hair before it (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.19">Eze 29:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.20">20</reference>).<div eID="gen13626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hired--</hi>alluding to Ahaz' hiring (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.7">2Ki 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.8">8</reference>) Tiglath-pileser against Syria and Israel; namely,<div eID="gen13627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13628" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by them beyond the river--</hi>namely, the Euphrates; the eastern boundary of Jewish geographical knowledge (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">Psa 72:8</reference>); the river which Abram crossed; the Nile also may be included (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Is 7:18</reference>) [G. V. Smith]. Gesenius translates, "With a razor hired in the parts beyond the river."<div eID="gen13628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">head ... feet--</hi>the whole body, including the most honored parts. To cut the "beard" is the greatest indignity to an Easterner (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Is 50:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sa 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.1">Eze 5:1</reference>). <div eID="gen13629" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fd70f545db28ed5c0561fc1047455a2eb3e7f6e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8448"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.7.21-Isa.7.25">Is 7:21-25</reference>. The Coming Desolate State of the Land Owing to the Assyrians and Egyptians.</title> <div sID="gen13630" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8448"/><hi type="bold">21. nourish--</hi>that is, own.<div eID="gen13630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">young cow--</hi>a heifer giving milk. Agriculture shall cease, and the land become one great pasturage. <div eID="gen13631" type="x-p"/>
entries.76af4bfceef834ee5b8f5c641912ca054f191e91: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8449"/><div sID="gen13632" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8449"/><hi type="bold">22. abundance--</hi>by reason of the wide range of land lying desolate over which the cows and sheep (including goats) may range.<div eID="gen13632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">butter--</hi>thick milk, or cream.<div eID="gen13633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honey--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.7.15">Is 7:15</reference>). Food of spontaneous growth will be the resource of the few inhabitants left. Honey shall be abundant as the bees will find the wild flowers abounding everywhere. <div eID="gen13634" type="x-p"/>
entries.23f5ce8a0c88ef896bc6fc5f9587ff752e8f4c1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8450"/><div sID="gen13635" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8450"/><hi type="bold">23. where there were, &c.--</hi>where up to that time there was so valuable a vineyard as to have in it a 1000 vines, worth a silverling (shekel, about 2s. 3d.; a large price) each, there shall be only briers (<reference osisRef="Song.8.11">So 8:11</reference>). Vineyards are estimated by the number of the vines, and the goodness of the kind of vine. Judea admits of a high state of cultivation, and requires it, in order to be productive; its present barrenness is due to neglect. <div eID="gen13635" type="x-p"/>
entries.867df8c6caaed23406296d3a0bb5abc232b1d6a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8451"/><div sID="gen13636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8451"/>24. It shall become a vast hunting ground, abounding in wild beasts (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jr 49:19</reference>). <div eID="gen13636" type="x-p"/>
entries.77cebb93473bc3684a8a546f9d768197174b6a9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8452"/><div sID="gen13637" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8452"/><hi type="bold">25. shall be--</hi>rather, "were once."<div eID="gen13637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">digged--</hi>in order to plant and rear vines (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.6">Is 5:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13639" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there shall not come--</hi>that is, none shall come who fear thorns, seeing that thorns shall abound on all sides [Maurer]. Otherwise, "Thou shalt not come for fear of thorns" [Gesenius]. Only cattle shall be able to penetrate the briery ground.<div eID="gen13639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lesser cattle--</hi>sheep and goats. <chapter eID="Isa.7"/>

entries.8190ab3db2a94c6bce52d92b109e1450627e5c8d: <div eID="gen26823" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26824" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26825" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26825" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26824" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26826" type="x-p"/> The king of Judah and the royal family being in the utmost consternation on receiving accounts of the invasion of the kings of Syria and Israel, the prophet is sent to assure them that God would make good his promises to David and his house; so that, although they might be corrected, they could not be destroyed, while these prophecies remained to be accomplished, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.1-Isa.7.9">Isa 7:1-9</reference>. The Lord gives Ahaz a sign that the confederacy against Judah shall be broken, which sign strikingly points out the miraculous conception of the Messiah, who was to spring from the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.10-Isa.7.16">Isa 7:10-16</reference>. Prediction of very heavy calamities which the Assyrians would inflict upon the land of Judea, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.17-Isa.7.25">Isa 7:17-25</reference>. <div eID="gen26826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26827" type="x-p"/> The confederacy of Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, king of Israel, against the kingdom of Judah, was formed in the time of Jotham; and perhaps the effects of it were felt in the latter part of his reign; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.37">2Kgs 15:37</reference>, and note on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.7-Isa.1.9">Isa 1:7-9</reference> (note). However, in the very beginning of the reign of Ahaz, they jointly invaded Judah with a powerful army, and threatened to destroy or to dethrone the house of David. The king and royal family being in the utmost consternation on receiving advises of their designs, Isaiah is sent to them to support and comfort them in their present distress, by assuring them that God would make good his promises to David and his house. This makes the subject of this, and the following, and the beginning of the ninth chapters, in which there are many and great difficulties. <div eID="gen26827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26828" type="x-p"/> Chap. 7 begins with an historical account of the occasion of this prophecy; and then follows, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.4-Isa.7.16">Isa 7:4-16</reference>, a prediction of the ill success of the designs of the Israelites and Syrians against Judah; and from thence to the end of the chapter, a denunciation of the calamities to be brought upon the king and people of Judah by the Assyrians, whom they had now hired to assist them. Chap. 8 has a pretty close connection with the foregoing; it contains a confirmation of the prophecy before given of the approaching destruction of the kingdoms of Israel and Syria by the Assyrians, of the denunciation of the invasion of Judah by the same Assyrians. <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Isa 8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.10">Isa 8:10</reference>, give a repeated general assurance, that all the designs of the enemies of God's people shall be in the end disappointed and brought to naught; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.11">Isa 8:11</reference>, etc., admonitions and threatenings, (I do not attempt a more particular explanation of this very difficult part), concluding with an illustrious prophecy <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1-Isa.9.6">Isa 9:1-6</reference>, of the manifestation of Messiah, the transcendent dignity of his character, and the universality and eternal duration of his kingdom.
entries.108e76daab5dc37d5f6a0bb017437fed4d76b675: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen26828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26829" type="x-p"/> Now - נא na, is omitted by two MSS., the Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic, and Vulgate.
entries.09d673acee46e86d744587eb80c16632078ced56: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen26829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26830" type="x-p"/> The Syriac omits וארם vearam, "and Syria;" the Vulgate reads מלך ארם melech aram, "king of Syria:" one or the other seems to be the true reading. I prefer the former: or, instead of וארם ובן vearam uben, read ופקח בן vepekach ben, and pekah son, MS.
entries.b8315d625692f8b44c1885efa1d19783c96feff8: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen26830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26831" type="x-p"/> Because - Remaliah - All these words are omitted by one MS. and the Syriac; a part of them also by the Septuagint.
